Zorchinsky c. SPHR Concordia

2024 QCCS 3646

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

PRESIDED BY the

______________________________________________________________________

ANASTASIA ZORCHINSKY

MICHAEL ESHAYEK

HILLEL CONCORDIA

THE START UP NATION

Plaintiffs

v.

SPHR CONCORDIA

INDEPENDENT JEWISH VOICES
CANADA INC.

MAHMOUD KHALIL

MONTRÉAL4PALESTINE

ALLIANCE4PALESTINE.QC

DIRECT ACTION MONTRÉAL NOW
/

DIRECT ACTION CONCORDIA

REEMA ABOUDRAZ

Defendants

and

CONCORDIA UNIVERSITY

Mise en cause

______________________________________________________________________

TRANSCRIPTION
OF REASONS EXPRESSED ORALLY OCTOBER 2, 2024
[1]

______________________________________________________________________

Preliminary comments

[
1
]

The Court will deliver an oral judgment. In doing so it will omit
most references in its notes to the exhibits and allegations on which it
relies. The Court reserves the right to insert those references from its notes
to complete the transcription of the reasons stated orally.

[
2
]

The Court issues oral reasons today given the urgency of the matter as
well as the closure of the Superior Courts (i) October 3 and 4, 2024 for the
annual assembly of Superior Court judges and (ii) Saturday October 5 and Sunday
October 6 aside from the service de garde offered 24/7. The next open day is
October 7 on which the events set out in the materials will take place.

[
3
]

The Court expresses itself in English as the entirety of the
materials, including the exhibits from all sources, are in English.

Application

[
4
]

Anastasia Zorchinsky (“
Zorchinsky
”) and Michael Eshayek (“
Eshayek
”)
are students registered students at Concordia University (“
Concordia
” or
(the “
University
”). Hillel Concordia (“
Hillel Concordia
”) is an
association and a registered student club at Concordia. The Start Up Nation (“
SUN
”),
an association and registered student group at Concordia.

[
5
]

Zorchinsky, Eshayek, Hillel Concordia and SUN (“
Plaintiffs
”)
have filed an October 1, 2024 originating Application for the issuance of a
provisional injunction and for a protection order invoking articles 141 and
following and 509 and following of the
Code of Civil Procedure
[2]
(“
C.C.P.
”). The
Application also includes conclusions for interlocutory orders at a later stage
and permanent orders after a hearing of the merits. The hearing today, however,
concerned the conclusions for provisional relief sought for a duration of ten (10)
days.

[
6
]

Plaintiffs have initiated their proceedings against a mix of
individuals, both current and former students, as well as incorporated and
unregistered unincorporated entities.

[
7
]

Solidarity for Palestinian Human Rights, Students for Palestine’s
Honour and Resistance and/or SPHR Concordia (“
SPHR Concordia
”)
[3]
is an unregistered,
unincorporated entity which purported to be a “student club” associated with
the Concordia Student Union (“
CSU
”)
[4]
.
On or about September 3rd, 2024, SPHR Concordia became an “independent club” because
Concordia forbade it from obtaining registered student group status
[5]
.

[
8
]

Independent Jewish Voices Canada Inc. (“
Independent Jewish Voices
Canada
”)
[6]

is a non-profit corporation registered under the
Canada Not-for-Profit
Corporations Act
[7]
.
On its website, it refers to itself as a “grassroots organization grounded in
Jewish tradition that opposes all forms of racism and advocates for justice and
peace for all in Israel-Palestine”.
[8]

Plaintiffs allege that it has been instrumental in organizing walkouts, riots,
blockades and hate rallies, creating and posting offensive posters and
graffiti, and engaging in violent, anti-social and hateful behavior on Campus.
[9]

[
9
]

Mahmoud Khalil (“
Khalil
”) and Montréal4palestine are closely
related and presented in the Application as such
[10]
. Khalil is a former Concordia
student who is said to have graduated in 2022
[11]
.
Plaintiffs allege that he is one of the leaders, if not the leader, along with
others of an unincorporated, unregistered entity known as Montréal4palestine (“
Montréal4palestine
”).
In addition to other allegations, Plaintiffs assert that Montréal4palestine
appears to be a Montréal chapter of a Canada-wide coordinated and organized
effort to rally masses with the intent to disturb in support and glorification
of ideologies and actions of organizations such as Hamas and Hezbollah.
[12]
Plaintiffs allege that Khalil
is not a Concordia student although he appears to be an alumnus, and Montréal4palestine
has no standing at Concordia.

[
10
]

Direct Action Montréal Now, also known as Direct
Action Concordia (“
Direct Action Concordia
”), is an unincorporated,
unregistered entity operating two (2) Instagram pages.
[13]
Plaintiffs allege that Direct
Action Concordia has no standing at Concordia.

[
11
]

Alliance4Palestine.QC (“
Alliance4Palestine.QC
”)
is an unincorporated, unregistered entity operating an Instagram page.
[14]

[
12
]

Reema Aboudraz (“
Aboudraz
”)
[15]
is a Concordia student with
an active Instagram profile and participation in media interviews, including
those posted to YouTube, expressing support for Palestinians and also Hamas.
[16]

[
13
]

SPHR Concordia, Independent Jewish Voices
Canada, Khalil, Montréal4palesting, Direct Action Concordia,
Alliance4Palestine.QC and Aboudraz are identified each as defendants to the
Application (“
Defendants
”).

[
14
]

Concordia is included as mise en cause. At the
hearing, it made no submissions and left the resolution of the Application to
the discretion of the Court.  It reserved it submissions in regard to the facts
alleged.

Observations

[
15
]

Having read the Application including the
affidavits filed in support of it when notified and the supplemental affidavits
provided after notification, and having read, viewed and listened to the
exhibits, the Court has four observations.

[
16
]

First, Zorchinsky and Eshayek (“
Student Plaintiffs
”)
are of the Jewish faith. Aside from one of the Defendants, namely Independent Jewish
Voices Canada, none of the other Defendants claim a link to the Jewish faith. Defendants
do share a common element regarding their solidarity for Palestinians.

[
17
]

Second, the Application has nothing to do with
the nature of the disagreements which might be anticipated between Plaintiffs
and Defendants. The Application is not about freedom of expression. The
Application seeks to permit Student Plaintiffs and the student club Hillel
Concordia and student group SUN to participate actively in their respective
capacities at Concordia. The Court notes that Plaintiffs have taken great care
to tailor the conclusions in a way which (i) safeguards Plaintiffs’ access to
Concordia in order to allow them to benefit from the public service offered by
one of Québec’s top universities and (ii) operates independent of the subject
matter of what Defendants may wish to express or images they may wish to
display (aside from threats of harm and violence).

[
18
]

Third, it would misread and misrepresent the
Application to claim that the purpose of the Application is to silence Plaintiffs.
Rather, as appears from the allegations and the conclusions, the purpose is to
protect access to and limit the interruption and disruptions of the very
activities which allow Concordia to present itself as a world class university.
Those accesses include the ability to attend academic classes and to circulate
freely on the grounds of the University without fear for one’s personal safety
and security. Plaintiffs do not mind hearing what Defendants have to say. They
only seek protection from behavior which constitutes intimidating and harassing
behavior.

[
19
]

Fourth, the court record at this stage is
expected to be incomplete. The proceedings at this stage are at their earliest
and include only the materials filed by Plaintiffs. Those materials include P-1
to and including P-50 and the affidavits filed in support of the Application.
The file containing the exhibits took over 5 minutes to download and comprised
text and pdf documents as well as videos including those generated by
Plaintiffs of Defendants’ various social media pages.

[
20
]

The Court expects at a later date that Defendants
may, if they choose to do so, provide their own allegations of fact and
exhibits in support of their version of the situation. For the purposes of
today, Defendants did not attend the trial hearing.  As appears from the
extensive set of exhibits, Defendants did, though, appear and participate by
way of the extensive set of text, visual and auditory elements of evidence
which they themselves created and circulated on and from their social media
accounts.

Nature of the proceeding

[
21
]

Plaintiffs apply for a provisional injunction
under
article 509

C.C.P.
which includes orders to refrain from or cease doing
something or to perform a specified act.

Article 509

C.C.P.
An injunction is an order of the
Superior Court directing a person or, in the case of a legal person, a
partnership or an association or another group not endowed with juridical
personality, its officers or representatives to refrain from or cease doing
something or to perform a specified act.

Such an injunction may direct a natural person to
refrain from or cease doing something or to perform a specified act in order to
protect another natural person whose life, health or safety is threatened. Such
an injunction, called a protection order, may be obtained, in particular, in a
context of violence, such as violence based on a concept of honour. A
protection order may only be issued for the time and on the conditions
determined by the court, without however exceeding three years.

A protection order may also be requested by another
person or a body if the threatened person consents to it or, failing that, with
the authorization of the court.

[
22
]

As appears from the above,
article 509

C.C.P.

also provides that the court may issue a protection order to protect an
individual whose life health or safety is threatened. The duration of the order
cannot exceed three years. That protection is sought to threats regarding Zorchinsky
and Eshayek and to govern Khalil and Aboudraz in their conduct.

[
23
]

Article 510

C.C.P.
provides that a provisional
injunction cannot be granted for a period exceeding ten (10) days absent the
consent of the parties.

Service

[
24
]

The Application, along with the notice of
presentation and summons, were notified by various means late yesterday. Those
means included traditional ones such as service by bailiff but also more
increasingly more common special modes such as social media. While the
Code
of Civil Procedure
makes special mention of service by bailiff, it does
authorize other methods of notification.

[
25
]

Article 110

C.C.P.
stipulates that the court can
authorize other modes of service either in advance of a hearing or at the
hearing. Notification can be made by, among others, (i) technological means and
(ii) by public notice. If the law requires notification be made by court
bailiff, it is called service. Whatever the method of notification used, a
person who acknowledges receipt of the document or admits having received it is
deemed to have been validly notified.

[
26
]

In the present case, Plaintiffs have accomplished
effective notification by way of (i) bailiff, (ii) a variety of technological
means and (iii) by public notice. At the beginning of the hearing, the Court examined
with counsel for Plaintiffs each of the modes of service in regard to each of
the Defendants. Aside from Khalil who was served at his residence
[17]
and the corporations which
had places of business identified in the CIDREQ, the other Defendants were
notified by various social media, including Instagram and Facebook. The Court
examined each of the proofs of service provided by the bailiffs who effected
each mode, be it in person by bailiff or through a bailiff by way of social
media.

[
27
]

These other modes are common in the special mode
of services currently authorized by the courts. In this particular case, based
on the exhibits filed in the court record, the Court determines that the
service by such social media channels is all the more appropriate and
effective. As appears from the exhibits, it is those very channels of social
media which justify the Application to the Court and identify exact channels
through which to contact each of the Defendants in charge of such channels. It
will be up to Defendants on the merits or at a later hearing to distance
themselves from their own social media. For the purposes of today, however, the
Court is satisfied that the special modes of service qualify as valid service.

[
28
]

If the Court had any doubt, which it does not,
service by way of public notice is confirmed by the social media posts made
subsequent to service on Instagram. Each of Plaintiffs filed as exhibit P-49
and P-50 an extract of the Alliance4Palestine.QC and extracts of its Instagram
page. That document is reproduced in the court record.

[
29
]

The Alliance4Palestine.QC Instagram page
contains a clear photo representation of the front page of the original
Application with a reproduction of other paragraphs such as paragraph 67, 68
and 69. Based on the nature of the exhibits already in the record and the
confirmation of this social media posting after service, the Court remains satisfied
that Defendants were properly notified and had due notice of the hearing today.
Defendants were properly notified among themselves by one of the Defendants
which constituted public notice.

[
30
]

The Court also used the courthouse address
system at two times in the hearing, one at the very onset and once in the
middle, in order to individually call each of the Defendants one-by-one to
direct them to the hearing room. Though no one showed up in person, the Court
did notice that the Team platform had at least 20 open accounts connected by Teams.

[
31
]

The Court also noted that the social media
postings also contained further postings by Alliance4Palestine.QC containing
photos of one of the counsel presenting for two of the Plaintiffs and
containing negative comments. This raised concerns that Alliance4Palesting.QC
was interfering with the representation of those Plaintiffs by their counsel.  The
postings by Alliance4Palestine.QC apposed a pair of emojis beside each of the
named Plaintiffs. The emojis associated them with either a rat, a pig, a donkey
or a cockroach and for each an emoji with the middle finger raised. They
expression was “Fuck all of you. We are in CANADA - not in your zionists supremacist
state, where you get to abuse and others have to zip it”.
[18]
The emojis included a pile of
poop and other comments not worthy of repetition.

[
32
]

The text confirms receipt of the Application and
a grasp, albeit inaccurate, regarding the nature of the conclusions sought
against Defendants.  As noted above, the purpose of the Application is not the
suppression of free speech but intimidating, threatening and harassing activities
which interrupt and disrupt access to the academic services and activities
offered by Concordia, including Hillel Concordia and SUN.

[
33
]

Based on the above, the Court determines that Defendants
were notified by channels to which they have regular access, absent proof from
them to the otherwise. As appears also from the materials, Alliance4Palestine.QC
is one of the channels by which public information is made. Based on all the
above, the Court is satisfied that notification has been affected not only by
technological means but also by public notice, with the assistance of
Alliance4Palestine.QC.

Service by special
mode

[
34
]

At the onset of the hearing, Court heard a written
application to authorize the service made yesterday. After reviewing the court record
and based on the submissions of counsel at the hearing, the Court granted and
authorized the special modes of service. The conclusions to that authorization are
broad and include the manners in which Defendants have used the social media as
evidenced from the exhibits before the Court. The Court did remove the mention
of service by “telecopy” as that seems to be an ineffective and unlikely manner
through which to notify the Defendants in this case. That order is stated to
apply to further steps in the file.

Review of the Application
and exhibit

[
35
]

The Court had the opportunity to read the entire
Application and all the exhibits prior to the hearing. This was because the materials
were provided to the Court at 17:00 on October 1. The Application comprises 38
pages and 130 paragraphs of allegations a fact and certain qualifications of law.
It is supported by the initial affidavits of the Student Plaintiffs and the
supplemental affidavits, as well as exhibits P-1 to and including P-50. The
notice of presentation and standard summons were also included at the same time
Plaintiffs notified the Application. The Court received also a link from which
it could download a digital copy of the exhibits.

[
36
]

Many of the exhibits comprised documents as well
as screenshots of social media. Some of the exhibits included videos. The Court
viewed the videos, without and with sound. It did so in order to separate the
content of what was being said from the manner in which it is being said. This
is because Plaintiffs reproach is not that they disagree with what is said, (other
than physical threats of violence) but the intimidating, threatening and
harassing way in which the images and the messages are communicated.
[19]

[
37
]

Those videos and images did reflect moments in
which any reasonable person would feel a valid, immediate and imminent fear to
their physical security. The images demonstrated that the common areas of the
university were obstructed by individuals, mostly concealed by scarves, hiding
their faces while blocking access or and circling a single individual or fewer
individuals around a greater circle of masked individuals.
[20]

[
38
]

A video posted to one Khalil’s Instagram accounts
@c43.mtl called Student Plaintiff Eshayek a “fucking faggot” and “the little
coward… ex IOF criminal, crying about being too scared to walk around campus”.
[21]
Khalil’s post ends with the
following:

And before anyone comes at me for my choice of words
…. Remember that that’s a full bragging IOF soldier in front of me. I can only
hold myself back from punching him square in the face right there and then.
There’s no holding back on anything else in that situation.
[22]

[
39
]

The common spaces that appear in those images,
along with the affidavits, demonstrate that these areas are how one would
access Concordia's pavilions, facilities and buildings in order to attend
academic activities in classrooms and lecture halls and activities offered by
clubs and groups such as the other such as those offered by Hillel Concordia
and SUN.

Reviewed the
conclusions

[
40
]

At the direction of the Court, Plaintiffs
presented the conclusions before pleading. The Court asked them to do so in
order to understand the goal of the Application. As already noted above, the
goal of the Application including the express conclusions, are designed to
ensure free access without intimidation threat or harassment to the facilities
of Concordia as well as a protection order. The facilities are identified as
buildings in the proceedings and include a lengthy list of addresses which help
any reader to understand the location which would be governed by the
proceedings. The Court attaches a list generated from paragraphs 2A and 2B at
pages three to seven of the Application. Those are described as the buildings
and the court will adopt that language. For the sake of clarity, the court
understands that the buildings will be more detailed in the conclusions sought
namely that the buildings are used to explain the location in the Application
but the conclusions refer to pavilion facility or building.

Evidence

[
41
]

it is true that the party the Court has only
heard from Plaintiffs at this stage. The unusual aspect of the case is that
virtually the entire majority of the exhibits are media which results from the Defendants
themselves. In other words it is not the words of the Plaintiffs which are
provided in evidence only but the bulk of the evidence is that which comes from
Defendants. The Defendants chose not to attend the hearing despite Dooley do
notification their own words and actions are well and extensively provided both
in words and in images and with audio in the record.

Four criteria

[
42
]

The Court must be satisfied that Plaintiffs meet
all four conditions applicable to the issuance of a provisional injunction.
[23]
These include urgency
appearance of right, irreparable prejudice and balance of convenience.

[
43
]

Such an order is a discretionary measure, issued
for conservatory purposes, in a situation of urgency, for a limited time and
with regard to a file where the responding party has not yet been able to
introduce all its arguments.
[24]

It is pronounced only in urgent and exceptional cases.

[
44
]

At this early stage of the proceedings, caution
is called for,

[25]
as
the only
prima facie
evidence in the file is the affidavits and exhibits
submitted by Plaintiffs. Because the procedural vehicle does not offer the
usual legal guarantees, the criteria of urgency and irreparable harm are of
great importance. They are the justification for proceeding summarily with the
safeguard order.

[26]

[
45
]

The clearer the right, the less the Court has to
consider the inconvenience to the other party if the order is granted.
Conversely, the less apparent the right, the greater the need for a careful
examination of the irreparable nature of the harm, and the greater the weight
of the inconvenience.
[27]
The conditions are interrelated
[28]
and the Court must examine them
in relation to each other, using a global approach
[29]
. The
Court will deal with each in turn.

Urgency

[
46
]

A key criterion which must be dealt with at this
stage is whether or not the issuance of a provisional injunction is urgent. The
Court determines that Plaintiffs have met their standard.

[
47
]

The evidence at this stage supports the determination
that it is more than probable, if not highly probable, that Defendants will
proceed next week
[30]

to engage in the very conduct which has already provided disturbing written,
visual and auditory evidence filed in the court record. Plaintiffs’ evidence,
including those exhibits which issue from Defendants themselves, provides
numerous examples, stemming from over the last year up to and including the
recent weeks, which involved the Defendants and their interruption and
disruption of the access to Concordia and the academic activities provided on
in the pavilions, facilities and buildings. Described as “context” in the
Application, the allegations and exhibits refer to not just the November 8,
2023 events but, most recently, the September 12 2024 disturbance and the
September 25 occupation. It is in that context which the allegations and exhibits
are understood.

[
48
]

Those events are clearly set out therein and
which individual Student Plaintiffs being surrounded by angry, verbally abusive
mobs and yelled at with expletives and commands to “get out”. The language was
not only intimidating but also included threats of physical violence. As noted,
the record includes threatening texts and social media postings which mention
that the authors “could not wait to see” Plaintiffs or that one of them would
be “too scared to walk around campus”. These messages are either posted by
Defendants or on their social media accounts.

[
49
]

The materials include a buffet of equally
troubling materials, and the Court need only focus on a few allegations
therein. The following allegations are focused on because they are
representative of the mass of evidence which emanates from Defendants
themselves.

[
50
]

Exhibit P-28 is a seven-page excerpt of postings
made by SPHR Concordia. P-28 refers to the successful disruption of ten classes
5 at McGill and five at Concordia. The posts underline that those five classes
were chosen because they are the “largest” ones at each university. The posts
attribute the activities of SPHR Concordia as a consequence of “the destruction
of every Gazan university”.
[31]

That that posting states that “[w]e act in support of these martyrs and our
fellow students in Gaza who cannot return to university.”
[32]

Defendants
state that the apparent solution then is “the blockade of the 5 largest classes
at Concordia.”
[33]

The posting continues that “[t]he culmination of our response meant that over 1,100
students were unable to attend classes across both campuses, paralyzing our
complicit institutions and reminding our administration that our campuses
belong to the students. we, the students, will not allow business or classes as
usual during genocide.
[34]

[
51
]

The post also speaks of “escalation” and the
undertaking sent to the message that the “administrators will continue to pay
dearly for their complicity”.
[35]

The newest messages alert further activities that will take place next week as
of October 7. The call to participate are set out in the exhibits at P-43 which
include a demand to have further impacts on class attendance. These events
comprise what is referred to as the “WEEK OF RAGE OCT 7-11” in P-28 and an
“October 7
th
Celebration”
[36]

of the events on October 7, 2023 in Israel.

[
52
]

Based on the context provided by the recent
exhibits which emanate from Defendants themselves and the satisfaction
expressed by Defendants with their recent prior results to interrupt and
disrupt academic activities the Court considers that Plaintiffs have clearly
met the criterion for the urgency, and this, even on a
quia timet
[37]
basis.

[
53
]

These same reasons apply to the protection order
and to the conclusion that the present judgment applies notwithstanding appeal.

Appearance of
right

[
54
]

Plaintiffs have established a clear and strong
right for which they seek the provisional injunction. Student Plaintiffs are
registered students at Concordia and have a right to pursue their education and
participate in related academic pursuits and activities at Concordia. They are
entitled to do so in an environment which is a university environment. That
environment is free from violence, harassment, obstruction and intimidation.
They also have a fundamental right to security add to be free from
discrimination and harassment under the
Québec
Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
.
[38]
Those rights are entitled to
protection.

[
55
]

Hillel Concordia and SUN each also have
established their right to operate and offer their activities without being
impacted by the upcoming activities planned by Defendants. Hillel Concordia and
SUN are entitled to continue to offer their activities to other students who
are members or interested in their activities. Efforts which thwart, interrupt
or disrupt their activities interfere with their rights to offer them.

[
56
]

As a registered student, Aboudraz is bound by
the
Code of Rights and Responsibilities
[39]

issued by Concordia. Section 30 prohibits threatening or violent conduct. Section
32 prohibits harassment. Section 36 prohibits discriminatory communications,
namely those which expose a person to hatred or contempt by reason of a
prohibited ground of discrimination, Section 43 prohibits obstruction or
disruption of activities.

[
57
]

Those obligations are in addition to those
already provided by the
Québec
Charter of Human Rights
and Freedoms
as well as article 1457 C.C.Q. Whether or not the other Defendants
are students or no longer students, they are bound by the rules which govern
conduct in the province of Québec. Those rules are not limited to or reduced by
Concordia’s
Code of Rights and Responsibilities
.

[
58
]

These same reasons apply to the protection order
and to the conclusion that the present judgment applies notwithstanding appeal.

Irreparable prejudice

[
59
]

Plaintiffs have established a prejudice which is
not compensable by a payment of money. Their prejudice is intangible and
qualifies as irreparable. They are entitled each day to be without fear for
their own safety and well-being and without risk to them losing access to the
academic activities to which they are registered and entitled two. The
disruption of their academic at roll is time sensitive and cannot be recaptured
at a later date or compensated by money. Interrupting their education or
destroy otherwise disrupting or delaying it jeopardizes their obtaining their
degrees and their related professional aspirations. They are entitled to be
free from harassment at anytime and not need to wait for a future date at which
they will be free from harassment.

[
60
]

Student Plaintiffs are entitled to pursue their
studies without threat of harassment and disruption. They are also entitled to
attend their studies and to be free from discrimination and harassment,
especially at a university campus. The Court reiterates that their objection is
not to having to hear what is being supported by Defendants but rather the
harassing and intimidating manner in which the communications are made in their
regard.

[
61
]

These same reasons apply to the protection order
and to the conclusion that the present judgment applies notwithstanding appeal.

Balance of inconvenience

[
62
]

The balance of inconvenience favours Plaintiffs.

[
63
]

Defendants will suffer no inconvenience by
abiding by basic rules of civility and good faith conduct, either r by the laws
of Québec having general application such as the
Charter of Human Rights and
Freedoms
and
articles 6
,
7
and
1457
of the
Civil Code of Qu
ébec
[40]

(“
C.C.Q.
”) or by Concordia's own
Concordia’s Code of
Rights & Responsibilities.
Article 6
C.C.Q. requires that every person,
including Defendants, is bound to exercise their civil rights in accordance
with the requirements of good faith.
Article 7
C.C.Q. provides that no right
may be exercised with the intent of injuring another or in an excessive an
unreasonable manner and therefore contrary to the quiet requirements of good
faith. The rights referred to in
articles 6
and
7
C.C.Q. include freedom of
expression and freedom of assembly.

[
64
]

These same reasons apply to the protection order
and to the conclusion that the present judgment applies notwithstanding appeal.

Conclusions

[
65
]

Based on the allegations of fact in the
Application, the exhibits P-1 to and including P-50, the October 1, 2024 affidavits
of the Student Plaintiffs and their supplemental affidavits, the Court
determines that Plaintiffs have met each of the four criteria for the issuance
of a provisional injunction for a duration of ten (10) days. The Court will
make certain modifications to the conclusions provided in Plaintiffs’ draft
order.

[
66
]

The Court understands that the practical effect
of granting the conclusions will have an effect beyond the Student Plaintiffs.
That effect will apply to the members of the student club and association,
Hillel Concordia, and the student organization and group, SUN. The conclusions
will benefit other students of any academic pursuit attending Concordia who
also wish to pursue their studies and do so at Concordia at which they are
registered.

Modifications to draft

[
67
]

Only the conclusions A to and including O in the
Application are at issue at this stage of the preceding. The Court agrees with
the ten (10) day limit which is compliant with
articles 509
and
510

C.C.P.

[
68
]

The conclusions at paragraphs (i) and (ii) of
the proposed conclusions at C are limited to what is strictly necessary.  They
govern access to the pavilions, facilities and buildings of Concordia and prohibit
conduct which qualifies as intimidating, threatening and/or harassing. The
third conclusion (iii) of C adds the probation of activity which obstructs the
delivery of courses or disturbs their flow. The Court has no changes to make to
those conclusions and will issue an order to that effect

[
69
]

The conclusions are neutral as to the content of
the communications and impose no editorial content on what is said or displayed.
The limitation is on whether the subject matter, whatever it be, does not
qualify as intimidation, threats or harassment, as set out in the exhibits

[
70
]

Regarding the protection order, the limitation
is to a five (5) metre distance. The Court exchanged with counsel for
Plaintiffs regarding the practical effect of creating the five (5) m distance.
The Court determines that a further limitation be imposed consisting of an
upper radius of 300 meters from Concordia’s pavilions, facilities and buildings.
The addresses which comprise the pavilions, facilities and buildings and identify
each by their full civic addresses are listed in the Annex attached to the
present judgment.

[
71
]

The Court understands that the protection sought
by Student Plaintiffs may be justified to a much larger range. The Court,
however, is cautious not to unduly eliminate limit how or where Defendants can
circulate. In particular, the Court lacks adequate information as to whether
Khalil and Aboudraz would conduct themselves in the same manner if they were
further away from Concordia's pavilions, facilities and buildings. As a result,
the Court will limit the five (5) m distance to being in effect within 300
metres of or in any pavilion, facility or building of Concordia as identified
by the addresses listed on the Annex to this judgment.

[
72
]

Those terms of pavilions, facilities and
building comprise what is understood to be the campus (comprising the Sir
George William campus and the Loyola campus) and includes classrooms and
lecture halls. Doing so will permit the protection order to encompass different
modes of public and private transit using to access including metro, commuter
train, bus lines and parking. This would satisfy the explanations provided in oral
submissions to allow Plaintiffs to have free access to the areas which comprise
Concordia’s campus and ensure that the protection allows them to can get to and
from Concordia.

[
73
]

The conclusions as modified are read aloud and
into the court record.  A copy of the conclusions appear on the p.v. and, after
signature, will be transmitted to counsel for the parties.

Judicial costs

[
74
]

Article 340

C.C.P.
provides that the party which
prevails is entitled to its costs. There are exceptions under
article 341
C.C.P.
None of those exceptions arise, however, and the Court will apply the default
rule that the parties succumbing to the Application made to the Court will pay
judicial costs.
